title: DAY 2
text: Day 2 of 3   |   5 contact hours including breaks   |   09:00 – 14:00
Includes project communication: stakeholders, reporting cadence and written updates
notes:
Open with a five-minute recall exercise from Day 1 rather than a summary: ask three people to state the nine workflow stages, the seven steps of the training cycle, and what to do when a guideline does not cover an item.
Set expectations: today is the heaviest day. It moves from quality into management, and the afternoon covers communication and escalation — the two areas where annotation projects most often fail for reasons that have nothing to do with annotation skill.
Collect any questions left open from yesterday and say when you will answer them.

title: How Today Runs
text: Five contact hours including one hour of breaks. Six modules, one group case study and a written escalation exercise.
Day 1 recall, outstanding questions, Day 2 objectives
Modules 2.1 – 2.2: guidelines, calibration, QA and QC
Module 2.3: planning, work breakdown and capacity
Module 2.4: production monitoring and management response
Module 2.5: project communication  |  Module 2.6: risk and escalation
Knowledge check, reflection and daily review
Group case study presentation and Day 2 review
A QA exercise, a clarification log, a production plan with a revised capacity estimate, a corrective-action plan and a written escalation message.
notes:
Point out that the afternoon block carries two modules. Keep the morning to time or communication gets squeezed, and it is the module participants are least likely to have covered elsewhere.
The group case study runs from 11:00 and is presented in the final block. Form groups of three to four before the first break so people are not organising themselves during exercise time.

title: From Doing the Work to Managing the Work
text: From Doing the Work to Managing the Work
Day 1 covered what annotation is and how to teach it. Today covers how it is controlled, planned, monitored and communicated.
Identify error patterns and corrective actions.
Interpret production data and act on it.
Plan who is told what, when and how.
Escalate with evidence and a recommendation.
THE THREAD RUNNING THROUGH ALL SIX MODULES

Most annotation projects do not fail because people cannot annotate. They fail because an ambiguity was not resolved, a variance was not noticed, or a problem was not communicated in time for anyone to act on it.
notes:
Frame the day around the callout: the failure modes are managerial and communicative, not technical.
Ask participants for one example from their own experience of a project that went wrong for a non-technical reason. Keep it to two or three contributions and refer back to them during the day.
Remind them that teach-back topics on Day 3 include conducting a calibration exercise, completing a daily production report and escalating a project issue — all covered today.

title: Annotation Quality and Calibration
text: Interpreting guidelines consistently, resolving ambiguity through calibration, and separating quality assurance from quality control.
notes: Begin with the Day 1 car-and-bus example. Ask: whose fault was that? Steer the answer away from the annotators and towards the specification and the absence of calibration. That reframing sets up both modules.

title: Reviewing Guidelines Before Production Starts
text: Guidelines should specify the labels, definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules, examples, edge cases and required output format.
Read the complete approved instructions.  Before starting production — not alongside it.
Identify problems in the text.  Unfamiliar terms, conflicting instructions and missing examples.
Record questions in a clarification log.  One written record, not scattered messages.
Obtain decisions.  From the authorised project or client contact, not from colleagues’ opinions.
Update the guidance or decision log as approved.  With an effective date.
Communicate the interpretation.  To every annotator and reviewer, not only the person who asked.
Test understanding through sample tasks.  Confirm the clarification actually landed.
WHY STEP 6 IS THE ONE THAT FAILS

A decision that reaches one annotator and not the rest produces exactly the inconsistency the clarification was meant to remove. Communication is part of the quality process, not an administrative afterthought.
notes:
Ask how many people have started annotating before reading the full guideline. Normalise the admission, then explain the cost: rework on everything produced before the gap was noticed.
Step 3, the clarification log, is a deliverable participants will produce in the exercise. Show an example if you have one from a live project, with client details removed.
The callout anticipates Module 2.5. Flag the link explicitly so the afternoon does not feel disconnected.

title: The Calibration Exercise –Using the GIGO
text: Incorrect use of an annotation tool.
A genuine ambiguity in the task.
Use the approved specification as the reference.
Where the specification is insufficient, escalate.
Never resolve a gap through unsupported assumptions.
Record the decision, the rationale and the date.
A short clarification log containing the issue, the decision, the rationale, the effective date and the communication status.
EACH CAUSE NEEDS A DIFFERENT FIX

A tool error needs demonstration. A knowledge gap needs coaching. A genuine ambiguity needs escalation. Applying the wrong remedy leaves the problem in place — which is why diagnosis comes before correction.
notes:
Run a live five-minute calibration if you have sample items ready. It is far more convincing than describing it.
When you compare results, resist announcing the right answer immediately. Ask each person to explain their reasoning first — that is how you find out which of the five causes you are dealing with.
Emphasise 'effective date' in the log. Work completed before the decision was communicated was not wrong at the time, and needs a separate decision about whether to correct it.Give all participants the same sample items, have them annotate independently, then compare results and diagnose every discrepancy.

title: Two Different Activities, Both Necessary
text: Quality is shared: trainers prevent errors through clear instruction, managers establish controls, annotators follow the specification, reviewers assess output.
Whether the process is designed and implemented to produce the required quality
Whether actual output meets the requirements
Standardising how a label is explained
Reviewing whether the label was applied correctly
DETECTION WITHOUT PREVENTION IS A TREADMILL
Finding errors after production is not enough if the underlying cause remains unresolved. If the same error keeps appearing, the problem is in quality assurance, not quality control.
Mostly in quality assurance. Clear instruction, worked examples and confirmed competency prevent errors that QC would otherwise have to find one at a time.
notes:
The distinction sounds academic until you ask participants where their own projects invest. Most invest almost entirely in QC and wonder why the error rate does not fall.
A useful question for the room: if your rework rate doubled next week, what would you change? If every answer is 'inspect more', point back to this table.
Connect to Day 1: the trainer's role sits on the assurance side, which is why the training cycle ends with confirmed competency rather than with the demonstration.

title: Six Errors You Will See Repeatedly
text: Six Errors You Will See Repeatedly
A bus is classified as a car under a specification that distinguishes them
Review the category definition and provide targeted practice
An object required by the task is omitted
Explain the omission rule and review affected work
A bounding box does not cover the required object
Demonstrate the boundary rule and reassess samples
Conduct calibration and document the approved interpretation
Correct the format and introduce appropriate validation
Investigate the cause, coach the worker and verify improvement
THE LAST ROW IS THE IMPORTANT ONE

A repeated error after explanation is a different problem from a first-time error. Explaining it again rarely works ; find out why the explanation did not land, then verify the improvement rather than assuming it.
notes:
Ask participants which of these six they see most often. In practice it is usually inconsistent interpretation and incorrect boundaries.
Note that five of the six corrective actions involve teaching or demonstrating. This is where the trainer role and the QA role meet.
On the repeated error: possible causes include an unclear explanation, a misunderstood term, a tool limitation, workload pressure or a genuine capability gap. Each needs a different response, and coaching someone who has a tool problem simply wastes both people's time.

title: The Basic Quality-Control Process
text: Confirm the approved guidelines and acceptance criteria.
Select work for review according to the project sampling plan.
Record the error type and supporting evidence.
Determine whether the issue affects individual items or a larger batch.
Initiate correction and review the corrected output.
Investigate recurring errors and introduce preventive measures.
Record the results and communicate lessons to the team.
STEP 5 DECIDES THE SIZE OF THE PROBLEM

An individual error is coaching. A batch-level error is a production stop, a scope assessment and a conversation with the client about timeline. Getting this judgement wrong is expensive in both directions.
notes:
Step 2 depends on a sampling plan existing. Ask whether participants' projects have one, and what happens when sampling is ad hoc — reviewers inspect what is easy to reach rather than what is representative.
Step 4, evidence, is what makes a QA finding actionable. 'Quality is poor' is not a finding. 'Twelve of forty sampled items in batch 7 used the wrong category, all on the same edge case' is.
Step 8 closes the loop back to training. Lessons that stay with the reviewer do not improve anything.

title: Understanding Quality Metrics
text: The appropriate metrics depend on the annotation task. They are not interchangeable.
The proportion of evaluated predictions or labels that are correct, where this metric is appropriate.
Measures used in suitable classification or detection tasks to evaluate different aspects of correct identification.
Consistency between annotators, interpreted with regard to the task and the agreement method used.
The proportion of submitted work accepted without correction.
The proportion of work requiring correction under a defined calculation.
The amount of work reviewed relative to the defined population.
HIGH AGREEMENT IS NOT THE SAME AS CORRECT

If everyone misunderstood the same instruction, agreement will be high and the data will still be wrong. Acceptance thresholds must come from the approved specification, not from a general training example.
notes:
Do not turn this into a statistics lesson. Participants need to know what each metric answers and when it misleads.
The callout is the trap worth dwelling on: inter-annotator agreement measures consistency, not correctness. A team trained on the wrong interpretation agrees perfectly.
Stress the final sentence. Trainees will ask 'what is a good score?' The honest answer is that it comes from the project specification, and a trainer who invents a threshold creates a problem for the project manager.

title: Planning, Capacity and Production Control
text: Defining the deliverable, breaking down the work, estimating capacity, setting milestones and acting on daily production data.
notes: Shift of register here. Ask who has planned a piece of work with a hard deadline and a fixed team, and what they found hardest. Usually the answer is estimating how much the team can actually produce.

title: Define the Deliverable, Then Break Down the Work
text: Define the Deliverable, Then Break Down the Work
Standard practice: define the intended outcome, plan the work, assign responsibility, monitor performance and respond to change.
The type and volume of data to be labelled.
The required quality level and acceptance criteria.
Eight activities, each with an owner
An owner, an expected output and a planned completion date. An activity without all three is an intention, not a plan.
TAILOR THE TOOLS TO THE PROJECT
A two-week, four-person assignment does not need the same apparatus as a six-month programme. The principles are constant; the paperwork should be proportionate.
notes:
Point out that the eight activities mirror the nine workflow stages from Day 1 — the same work, viewed as a plan rather than as a process.
The first callout is worth writing on a flipchart. Most plans participants bring to the exercise will have activities with no named owner, and the resulting gaps are easy to demonstrate.
The second callout pre-empts the objection that this is too heavy for small jobs. Agree with it, and say what must survive even on the smallest job: who owns it, what counts as done, and when.

title: Estimating What the Team Can Actually Produce
text: Estimating What the Team Can Actually Produce
trained workers  ×  productive hours per worker per day  ×  planned production days
REQUIRED AVERAGE ACCEPTED OUTPUT PER DAY
remaining accepted volume  ÷  remaining production days
THESE ARE A STARTING POINT, NOT A FORECAST
Update the calculation using actual production and quality results. An estimate built before production and never revised is the most common cause of a deadline missed without warning.
Plan against work that passes quality control. Planning against submitted volume hides the rework and produces a forecast that collapses in the final week.
notes:
Work a real number on the flipchart: four annotators, six productive hours, ten days = 240 productive hours. Then ask what happens when one person is on leave for two days and the rework rate is 20 per cent.
'Productive hours' is not the length of the working day. Briefings, breaks, platform downtime and clarification waiting time all come out of it. Six productive hours from an eight-hour day is a realistic starting assumption, but it must be verified against actual data.
The second callout is the point participants most often get wrong in the afternoon exercise.

title: Checkpoints and Who Does What
text: SEVEN MILESTONES THAT REVEAL DELAY EARLY
This allocation is an example for training. Actual accountability must follow the agreed project structure, and a RACI that contradicts the real structure causes more confusion than it removes.
notes:
Milestones matter because they turn a distant deadline into a series of near ones. Ask what the warning signal is if 'platform ready' slips by three days — the delivery date has already moved, whether or not anyone has said so.
On RACI: the common failure is more than one 'Accountable' for the same activity, which in practice means nobody is. Check the participants' own projects against that.
The callout matters in an ITC context where the structure spans organisations. Agree the matrix with the project owner before publishing it.

title: Reading a Daily Production Report
text: A daily report should show planned output, actual output, quality, available capacity and unresolved issues. The figures below are illustrative.
Accepted output is well below plan
Unresolved questions may be blocking work
READ THE FIGURES TOGETHER, NOT ONE AT A TIME

Submitted output is down 15 per cent but accepted output is down 24 per cent, rework has risen by 70 per cent and twelve questions are unanswered. This is not a speed problem ; it reads as an unresolved guideline ambiguity.
Instructing annotators to work faster would increase submitted volume, increase rework further and reduce accepted output. The wrong diagnosis makes the number worse.
notes:
Do not give the interpretation away. Show the table, cover the right-hand column and ask the group what they think is happening and what they would do first.
Drive the group towards the twelve outstanding clarifications. That is the causal thread: unanswered questions lead to guessing, guessing leads to rejection, rejection consumes capacity that was planned for new production.
This table reappears in the group case study, so leave participants with the method rather than the answer.

title: Seven Steps, and a Note on Productivity Rules
text: Seven Steps, and a Note on Productivity Rules
RECOMMENDED MANAGEMENT RESPONSE TO A VARIANCE
Confirm the accuracy of the report.  Before acting on a number, establish that it is right.
Identify the main causes of the variance.  Guideline clarity, capacity, platform availability, QA findings.
Determine the effect on the deadline.  Recalculate required daily accepted output.
Assign corrective actions.  With named owners and due dates.
Update the delivery forecast.  Using actual production and quality data, not the original estimate.
Escalate what exceeds your authority.  Scope, cost, deadline and contractual changes.

Where a project uses basepoints or minimum productivity rules, trainers must explain the applicable rule and how performance is measured, including how quality, downtime and task complexity are handled.
COMPANY PRACTICE IS NOT AN INDUSTRY STANDARD
Teach Datamaker’s internal rules as company-specific procedures. Verify the current requirement for the relevant project before you teach it.
notes:
Step 1 sounds trivial and is skipped constantly. Reports contain mis-keyed figures, double counting and items logged against the wrong batch. Acting on a wrong number destroys credibility.
Step 6 is about authority, not courage. Decisions on scope, cost and deadline usually sit with the project owner or client. A manager who absorbs those decisions silently removes the client's chance to choose.
On basepoints: be careful here. Trainers who present an internal productivity rule as a universal standard create expectations that other projects will not honour. Always state that the rule is project-specific and check the current figure before teaching it.

title: Project Communication
text: Who needs to know what, when, through which channel, and in what form. The discipline that holds planning, quality and escalation together.
notes:
Open with a question rather than a definition: think of a project problem you have seen. How long was it between someone first knowing about it and the person who could fix it being told? That gap is what this module is about.
Make the case plainly: communication is the only one of today's topics that every participant will use every single working day.

title: Most Project Failures Are Communication Failures
text: Most Project Failures Are Communication Failures
The information usually exists somewhere in the team. The failure is that it did not reach the person who could act on it, in time, in a form they could use.
A guideline change reaches some annotators and not others.
A blocker is mentioned in passing and never logged.
A client is told a deadline is safe when it is not.
A report is accurate but arrives after the decision.
An update describes activity but not status.
Timely: it arrives while the recipient can still act.
Accurate: figures are verified before they are sent.
Specific: it names the work, the number and the date.
Actionable: it states what is needed and from whom.
Recorded: it exists in writing, not only in a conversation.
THE DAILY STANDARD FOR THIS PROGRAMME

Share progress proactively, raise issues early, respond to colleagues and keep project records updated every working day. Clear, timely and constructive communication carries the same weight as technical output.
When a manager hears nothing, they assume the plan is holding. An annotator who is blocked and says nothing has effectively reported that everything is fine.
notes:
The five failures in the left card map directly onto earlier modules: the guideline change is Module 2.1, the unlogged blocker is Module 2.6, the report arriving late is Module 2.4. Point the connections out.
'Silence is a message' is worth a minute of discussion. Many trainees believe they should only speak up when something is finished or when they are certain. Correct that explicitly: early partial information beats late complete information.
For trainers: tell participants they must teach this to annotators, not just practise it themselves. Annotators often have no model of what a good update looks like because nobody has ever shown them one.

title: Who Is Told What, When and How
text: Who Is Told What, When and How
Task allocation, guideline decisions, quality feedback
Short stand-up plus written note in the project record
Sampling priorities, recurring error patterns, rework volumes
Production against plan, blockers, revised forecast
Competency gaps, coaching needs, guideline misunderstandings
Milestone status, quality results, risks and decisions needed
Written report through the single point of contact
Logged incident with evidence and impact
AGREE THE CADENCE BEFORE PRODUCTION STARTS
A reporting arrangement settled during a crisis is settled badly. Confirm the audiences, the frequency, the format and the single point of client contact as part of project intake.
notes:
Walk the table by column, not by row: first who, then what, then when, then how. Participants build their own version for the case study.
The 'single point of contact' rule for client communication is the one to stress. Multiple people contacting a client with different versions of status is how teams end up having committed to things nobody agreed to.
Ask participants who the equivalent audiences are on their own projects, and whether any audience in the table currently receives nothing.

title: Writing an Update People Can Act On
text: Writing an Update People Can Act On
Status: where the work stands against plan, in numbers.
Change: what has moved since the last update.
Problem: what is blocking or threatening delivery.
Action: what has already been done about it.
Request: what you need, from whom, and by when.
Lead with the conclusion, not the chronology.
Use figures, not adjectives: "47 of 200", not "good progress".
Separate fact from assessment and label which is which.
Name owners and dates for every action.
Keep it short enough to be read on a phone.

Weak: "Annotation is going well but there are a few issues with the guidelines."  |  Strong: "Day 4 of 10. Accepted 680 of a planned 900 items. Rework is at 20 per cent, driven by the vehicle-category ambiguity. Twelve clarifications are outstanding; I have escalated them to the client contact and asked for a decision by Thursday. If the decision slips past Thursday, delivery moves by two days."
TEACH THE FORMAT, NOT THE INSTINCT
Trainees will not naturally write this way. Give them the five headings as a template and have them use it until it becomes habit.
notes:
Read both versions of the worked example aloud. The difference lands immediately when heard.
Draw out what the strong version gives the reader that the weak one does not: position against plan, the cause, the action already taken, the decision needed, the deadline for that decision and the consequence of missing it.
Short exercise if time allows: give the group the weak sentence and five minutes to rewrite it using the five-part structure. It is a strong candidate for a Day 3 teach-back topic.

title: Changes, Meetings and Handover
text: Confirm the decision is approved and authorised.
State the change, the reason and the effective date.
Give a worked example of the old and new treatment.
Say explicitly whether completed work must be corrected.
Record it in the decision log and confirm receipt.
Daily stand-up: done, next, blocked. Fifteen minutes.
Weekly review: plan versus actual, quality, risks, forecast.
Every meeting ends with actions, owners and dates.
Decisions are written down, not remembered.
No decision is made with the decision-owner absent.
What was completed and what remains.
Open clarifications and who holds them.
Known quality issues and affected batches.
Anything time-critical in the next 24 hours.
Written, not verbal — shifts and people change.
THE EFFECTIVE DATE IS NOT OPTIONAL
Without it nobody can tell which work was produced under which rule, and a correction exercise becomes guesswork across the whole dataset.
CONFIRM RECEIPT, DO NOT ASSUME IT
Sending a message is not communicating. Until someone has acknowledged a guideline change, assume the team is still working to the old rule.
notes:
The guideline-change procedure is the practical consequence of everything in Module 2.1. Run it as a short role-play if time allows: one participant announces a category change to the group, and the group identifies what was missing.
On meeting discipline: the daily stand-up format 'done, next, blocked' is easy to teach to annotators and surfaces blockers in a single sentence.
Handover matters in a training centre where different facilitators cover different cohorts. A verbal handover that stays verbal is lost the moment somebody is absent.

title: Risk, Issues and Escalation
text: Identifying operational risks, recording issues, and escalating with enough evidence for someone else to make a decision.
notes: Define the distinction up front: a risk might happen, an issue has happened, and a change alters the agreed basis of the work. Participants mix these constantly, and the response to each is different.

title: Risk, Issue, Change or Incident?
text: A client may delay approval of a guideline
Track the dependency and establish a decision deadline
Log the incident, identify affected work and seek technical support
Forecast review requirements and arrange suitable capacity
A label definition changes during production
Assess the impact and obtain the required approval
Follow the applicable security procedure immediately
The risk, its potential impact, the owner, the mitigation, the trigger and the contingency.
The problem, affected work, priority, owner, next action and expected resolution date.
SECURITY INCIDENTS DO NOT WAIT FOR THE DAILY REPORT
A suspected security or data-protection incident follows the applicable procedure immediately, regardless of reporting cadence.
notes:
Work through the table by asking the group to classify each situation before you reveal the type.
The frequent error is treating a risk as an issue (panicking about something that has not happened) or an issue as a risk (logging something that is already affecting production as a future possibility).
On the security row: participants handle trainee and project data. Make sure they know where their applicable procedure lives and who to contact, and that reporting promptly is required rather than optional.

title: Seven Parts of a Useful Escalation Message
text: Seven Parts of a Useful Escalation Message
Problem: what has happened, or what may happen.
Evidence: what information supports the assessment.
Impact: how quality, schedule, cost or delivery could be affected.
Actions taken: what has already been done.
Recommendation: which option is preferred, and why.
Decision required: who must decide, and by when.
PARTS 5, 6 AND 7 ARE WHAT DISTINGUISH ESCALATION FROM COMPLAINT
Reporting a problem transfers worry. Presenting options with a recommendation and a decision deadline transfers a decision - which is the only thing that moves the project forward.
notes:
Most escalations participants have seen stop at part 3. Make the point that a manager who receives parts 1–3 has to do the analytical work again before they can act.
Part 7 is routinely omitted and is the most important. Without a named decision-maker and a deadline, the message sits unread and the project continues towards the problem.
Participants write an escalation message in the group exercise. Assess it against these seven parts and give written feedback, because this is one of the Day 3 teach-back topics.

title: The Case Study
text: Production is below plan, quality errors are increasing and several workers are waiting for clarification. Work in groups of three to four.
A list of the most important issues and risks.
A corrective-action plan with owners and dates.
A short escalation message using the seven parts.
Who needs to be told, and what each audience needs.
The cadence and the channel for each audience.
The wording of the guideline-change notice.
The single point of contact for the client.
How you will confirm the message was received.
Is the diagnosis supported by the evidence?
Is the revised forecast arithmetically sound?
Would the escalation let a manager decide?
Does the communication plan reach everyone affected?
ASSESS THE THINKING, NOT THE SLIDES
The facilitator should assess the evidence, logic and practicality of the recommendations, not simply the quality of the presentation.
ALLOW 50 MINUTES, THEN 25 MINUTES FOR PRESENTATIONS AND FEEDBACK
Give each group five minutes to present and five for questions. Written feedback goes into the individual trainer assessment record.
notes:
Hand out the case figures from Module 2.4 as the starting data. Groups will need the planned and actual numbers in front of them.
Circulate during the exercise and listen for the diagnosis. Groups that jump straight to 'add more annotators' have not read the rework and clarification figures together ; prompt them rather than correcting them.
Keep the presentations strictly to five minutes. The discipline of a short, evidence-led briefing is itself part of what is being taught.
Record observations against each participant for the Day 3 assessment.

title: Review and Look Ahead
text: A clarification log from the calibration exercise.
A completed QA exercise with error classification.
A production plan and revised capacity estimate.
A corrective-action plan with owners and dates.
A written escalation message and communication plan.
What is the difference between quality assurance and quality control?
Why can high inter-annotator agreement still mean poor data?
What are the five parts of a written status update?
What three things does every activity in a plan need?
What makes an escalation actionable rather than informational?
Day 3 covers training design, adult-learning technique, competency assessment and the teach-back. Each participant delivers a short lesson and is assessed.

Choose your teach-back topic from today’s or yesterday’s material and bring a draft lesson plan. Strong candidates: running a calibration exercise, completing a daily production report, or escalating a project issue.
notes:
Run the review questions as a round-robin, not a lecture. If the QA/QC distinction or the five-part update structure is shaky, spend five extra minutes now rather than discovering it during the teach-backs.
Push participants to commit to a teach-back topic before they leave and write the choices down. People who decide overnight arrive without a plan.
Remind them that the teach-back is 35 per cent of the programme assessment — the single largest component — and that preparation is visible in the first thirty seconds.

title: Thank You
text: Training of Trainers  ·  AI Data Labelling, Quality Assurance and Project Operations  ·  International Trade Centre–Kenya × datamaker.
notes:
Final slide. Keep the close short.
Confirm three practical things before people leave: that assessment records and action plans have been collected, who to contact with follow-up questions, and the date of any planned follow-up or reassessment session.
